paper_title: VidDub: Replacement-Aware Distillation for Two-Step Video Dubbing

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Video dubbing aims to synthesize lip movements that match target speech while preserving the speaker identity, head pose, and background of a source video. Existing editors are predominantly trained via self-reconstruction under original paired audio, even though the source mouth becomes a conflicting target when driving speech is replaced. We introduce replacement-aware cross-audio supervision: paired-audio samples use full-frame reconstruction, whereas unpaired replacement-audio samples mask out source-mouth reconstruction losses and supervise the mouth solely through audio-visual synchronization while preserving unmasked facial regions and background. Because offline dubbing provides the complete source video and target speech beforehand, we present VidDub, a full-context diffusion editor distilled into two denoising steps (2 NFE). Our replacement-aware teacher first learns accurate lip synchronization without regressing toward conflicting source mouth movements. Matched trajectory regression then transfers the teacher's CFG-guided trajectories to a two-step student, and distribution matching distillation recovers visual quality after step compression. We will release the curated training dataset, VidDub-Bench, fixed paired- and cross-audio evaluation manifests, preprocessing outputs, and unified evaluation code. Across three training seeds, masking out conflicting source-mouth reconstruction improves cross-audio Sync-C by 0.833; the final two-step model combines strong lip synchronization with superior visual quality, identity preservation, and visual speech recognition across four benchmarks.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Video dubbing synthesizes lip movements that match replacement speech while preserving the speaker identity, 1 head motion, and scene of source video. Feed-forward and inpainting-based editors [5, 31, 57] and recent latent-space and diffusion-based editors [21, 28, 30, 54] have substantially improved visual fidelity, while few-step distillation reduces iterative sampling cost [24, 34, 37, 49, 50]. However, their primary training objective remains same-audio self-reconstruction: the model receives the original paired speech and is supervised to reproduce the mouth motion already present in the source video. This objective does not directly match the test-time task of dubbing, which requires replacing mouth articulation under new speech while leaving all other visual content unchanged. The core challenge lies in the supervision conflict between same-audio reconstruction and cross-audio dubbing. Under original paired speech, the source mouth, identity, pose, and background all serve as consistent ground-truth targets. Under unpaired replacement speech, the source mouth articulates different content and directly conflicts with the target audio, whereas the unmasked face and background Standard reconstruction remain valid ground truth. losses do not distinguish between these two regimes, and few-step distillation cannot recover accurate cross-audio lip synchronization if the teacher is penalized for deviating from the source mouth. Moreover, evaluation protocols centered on short same-audio clips fail to expose this discrepancy. We therefore study how to train cross-audio lip synchronization without the resulting model into two denoising steps, and evaluate it systematically across video domains and durations. target conflict, distill We propose VidDub, starting with replacement-aware cross-audio supervision. For paired same-audio samples, we apply standard full-frame reconstruction losses. For unpaired replacement-audio samples, we mask out flow-matching, pixel, and perceptual reconstruction losses inside the mouth region, preserve the unmasked face and background via spatial reconstruction, and supervise mouth articulation with an audiovisual synchronization loss. This decoupled formulation turns cross-audio dubbing into well-posed local editing task: target speech drives lip articulation, while the source video anchors identity, head pose, and background. We then distill the replacement-aware full-context teacher into full-context two-step student. Matched sameand cross-audio trajectories transfer the teachers CFG-guided predictions while preserving bidirectional temporal attention across the video window, and guided distribution matching distillation restores visual realism after step compression [49]. This architecture aligns with offline video dubbing, where the complete source video and target speech are available prior to inference. controlled same-backbone ablation in Table 11 demonstrates that block-causal conversion reduces first-frame latency for streaming, whereas full-context bidirectional attention achieves higher offline throughput, lower peak memory, and better visual speech recognition; VidDub therefore retains full-context bidirectional modeling. We evaluate VidDub across diverse cross-audio and crossdomain benchmarks. VidDub-Bench (Sec. 4.2) provides 256 speaker-disjoint generated videos with fixed sameand crossaudio pairings, structured prompt metadata, preprocessing outputs, and unified evaluation code. We will also release the curated training clips developed in this work. Together with Long-20, independent visual speech recognition (VSR) [25], temporal offset calibration, non-mouth preservation metrics, and four evaluation benchmarks, our protocol jointly assesses lip-reading intelligibility, temporal synchronization, visual fidelity, and minute-long stability [3, 8, 56]. Across three training seeds, masking out conflicting source-mouth reconstruction yields +0.833 0.040 cross-audio Sync-C improvement. Using only two denoising steps (2 NFE), VidDub achieves state-of-the-art cross-audio synchronization while improving VSR accuracy, identity preservation, and video quality over its matched causal counterpart. Replacement-aware cross-audio supervision resolves the cross-audio target conflict by masking out sourcemouth reconstruction losses under unpaired replacement speech while preserving unmasked facial regions and target-audio synchronization constraints. Full-context two-step diffusion distillation transfers matched sameand cross-audio teacher trajectories into bidirectional two-step student (2 NFE), followed by distribution matching distillation for improved visual quality while retaining full-context temporal attention. Open training dataset and evaluation benchmark contribute 85,435 curated training clips and VidDub-Bench with fixed sameand cross-audio pairings, unified evaluation scripts, and comprehensive VSR, temporal-alignment, preservation, perceptual, and long-video evaluations.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Visual speech generation and editing. Source-video dubbing methods edit mouth motion in existing footage to match target speech [5, 14, 21, 28, 30, 31, 43, 54, 57, 61], personspecific neural rendering methods fit subject from video [13, 29, 48], reference-conditioned portrait animation synthesizes head motion from an identity image, optionally with an additional pose source [4, 10, 12, 26, 36, 4547, 53, 59], and audio-driven generators synthesize talking faces from speech without an identity reference [38]. Unlike standard self-reconstruction training that penalizes deviations from the source mouth, our replacement-aware objective masks out source-mouth reconstruction on unpaired audio clips during training. Few-step video diffusion. Progressive, consistency, adversarial, and distribution-matching distillation methods accelerate diffusion sampling [24, 34, 35, 37, 49, 50]. Causal Forcing [58, 60] and Lip Forcing [6] combine autoregressive causal attention with few-step distillation for online 2 Figure 2: Full-context two-step dubbing architecture. Masked source frames and reference image preserve speaker appearance and pose, target-audio tokens drive lip articulation, and bidirectional self-attention jointly denoises the complete latent window in two steps. streaming. In contrast, offline video dubbing provides the full source video and replacement audio prior to generation. We retain full-window bidirectional attention while distilling the CFG-guided teacher into two-step student [16, 22]. Dubbing benchmarks and evaluation metrics. HDTF, VoxCeleb2, and TalkVid-Bench provide high-resolution and in-the-wild speech domains [3, 8, 56]; we extend evaluation to generated footage with explicit motion analysis. In addition to SyncNet-based synchronization [7], we use an independently trained visual speech recognizer [25] to evaluate lip-reading intelligibility alongside pixel fidelity, identity similarity [11], head pose accuracy [18], FVD [42], and 60-second temporal stability.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: Overview. Given source video and replacement speech, VidDub synthesizes synchronized lip movements while preserving speaker identity, head pose, and background. Our core insight is that ground-truth reconstruction targets must be decoupled by region when the driving speech is replaced. Figure 2 illustrates our bidirectional editing architecture, which conditions on masked source frames, reference frame, and frame-aligned audio tokens. Figure 3 presents the three-stage training pipeline: (a) replacement-aware teacher training, (b) two-step guided trajectory regression, and (c) distribution matching distillation. Sections 3.13.3 detail each component.

sections.title: 3.4 Long-Video Inference
sections.content: Long videos are processed using overlapping 81-frame windows conditioned on the corresponding source frames. Each window uses two denoising steps; consecutive windows advance by 64 frames and blend the 17-frame overlap. This sliding-window scheme bounds computation and memory while retaining bidirectional context within each window. Relation to causal few-step methods. Lip Forcing [6] represents the causal two-step design paradigm, and Causal Forcing develops causal ODE/DMD objectives [58, 60]. Our controlled same-backbone comparison shows that causal attention reduces first-frame latency but does not improve offline throughput or output quality. VidDub therefore combines replacement-aware cross-audio supervision with direct full-context distillation.

sections.content: Table 10 scores every 5 window and the final 5 segment. VidDub maintains the strongest mean and final synchronization across all 20 sequences while achieving the lowest non-mouth and color changes. The stable first-to-last preservation measurement shows that overlapping-window two-step inference maintains replacement-speech synchronization and source appearance over 60 seconds. Table 11 compares temporal attention designs under the same backbone, two-step budget, training data, and evaluation protocol. Causal execution reduces first-output latency to 1.052 by emitting 9-frame blocks progressively, which is advantageous for online streaming. For offline dubbing, where the complete source video and replacement speech are available beforehand, full-context execution processes an 81-frame window faster (11.3 vs. 9.4 FPS), reduces peak memory by 37% (13.77 vs. 21.96 GiB), wins all six independent VSR comparisons, and improves identity preservation. Combined with lower FVD on three of four benchmarks at closely matched cross-audio Sync-C (Tables 13), these results directly motivate our full-context two-step design.

sections.title: E Bidirectional Teacher Training
sections.content: E.1 Training chain The teacher follows three semantic stages matching the mainpaper figure: audio-conditioning warm-up trains only the audio adapter, joint editing adaptation updates DiT, VACE, and the adapter, and replacement-aware teacher refinement adds replacement audio and synchronization supervision behind DiT LoRA [17]. The resulting EMA state at step 200 is the parent used throughout the paper. Two independent auxiliary branches study quality-only refinement and replacement refinement after that quality-only branch; neither is an ancestor of the teacher. Table 16 lists the settings recorded in each runs saved arguments. Full denotes direct DiT optimization; LoRA-64 denotes frozen DiT base with rank-64 adapters merged at export. The 81-frame training statement in the main method applies to joint adaptation, replacement-aware refinement, causal adaptation, and distillation; the adapter-only initialization uses 49-frame clips. Teacher refinement and both auxiliary branches use mouth LPIPS weight 0.1 on same-audio samples and representation alignment at transformer layer 8 with weight 0.1. The replacement-aware branches add synchronization weight 0.02 for σ 0.8 and EMA 0.99. Same-audio and cross-audio scores are never pooled. Temporal-shift calibration. For 40 VidDub-Bench crossaudio outputs per method, we shift the waveform by {0, 1, 2, 3, 5} video frames and rerun the same evaluator. The estimated offset changes by exactly throughout 3 for every method. At zero shift, the Causal two-step VidDub, its teacher, and LatentSync return offset zero on all 40 clips. This is the temporal-shift test summarized in the main paper. Independent visual speech recognition. Driving utterances are transcribed with Whisper-large-v3 [33], while generated video is read by the visual-only LRS3 model of Ma et al. [25]; this reader shares no weights or objective with either the frozen training synchronizer or SyncNetv2. The final benchmark uses the 30/28/121 English HDTF/VoxCeleb2/VidDub-Bench clips reported in the main paper. sections.title: M Blinded Human Evaluation
sections.content: This completed study evaluates the final full-context VidDub model. Fifteen bilingual participants each completed all 150 anonymized A/B trials covering 50 generated sources and three opponents. Each trial asks which video is better in lip synchronization, mouth realism, identity preservation, temporal stability, and overall quality. Left/right assignment and the order of the first four criteria are randomized; overall quality is always shown last. The interface exposes neither method identity nor metrics. sections.content: The reproducibility package is defined by frozen split manifests, preprocessing thresholds, exact model and code revisions, checkpoint hashes, optimizer and EMA state, inference schedules, metric versions, failed-sample accounting, and commands used to generate every table and supplementary video. sections.title: O Ethical Considerations

VidDub edits source video and can make real person appear to say words they never said. We use only public research benchmarks and generated H3 subjects for figures; no private recordings of identifiable people are released. We will not redistribute source media whose licenses or consent basis do not permit redistribution, and will publish dataset/model card documenting provenance, permitted use, and removal-request channel before releasing artifacts. Model access will require use agreement forbidding non-consensual impersonation; released outputs will include provenance metadata, and detector baselines will accompany the model.
